---
title: "Overview"
---




Evaluating a malaria intervention takes two steps. The first is to estimate how intense
transmission is in the setting, and the second is to predict how prevalence and clinical
cases respond to a change in nets, spraying, or larviciding. MINTverse does both with
trained models that stand in for a full individual-based simulation. There are two
packages.

| Package | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `estimint` | Maps a measured prevalence to the entomological inoculation rate (EIR), relates EIR to the human biting rate (HBR), and estimates how EIR shifts when mosquito density changes. |
| `stateMINT` | Emulates the individual-based model. Given a setting and an intervention package, it returns the prevalence and case trajectories over the campaign. |

Use `estimint` on its own if you only want transmission intensity, and `stateMINT` on its
own if you already have an EIR and want a trajectory. One call, `run_scenarios`, chains
them. It derives net effectiveness from the net mix and the resistance level, calls the
`estimint` models for the EIR, and hands the result to the emulator.

`pip install estimint mintstate` installs both packages. The distribution you install is
called `mintstate`, but the module you import is `stateMINT`.

## Why an emulator

The trajectories `stateMINT` returns are those of an individual-based malaria
transmission model, the same model lineage implemented in the departmental
[`malariasimulation`](https://mrc-ide.github.io/malariasimulation/) package. That
simulation is detailed and slow. A single scenario takes minutes of computation, and
exploring an intervention space, or fitting to a survey, means running it thousands of
times.

`stateMINT` is trained on a large library of those simulation runs, and reproduces their
output in a few milliseconds per scenario on a CPU. At that speed you can sweep hundreds of
intervention packages, or back-calculate transmission from a survey, in the time the
simulation would take for one run.

The figure below is the whole stack running on a strongly seasonal parameter set that was held
out of training, plotted against the simulator it replaces. Its error is close to the emulator's
average across the whole held-out split.


::: {#986c026c .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.0, 3.3))
for ax, predictor, ylab in zip(axes, ("prevalence", "cases"),
                               ("prevalence", "cases per 1000 per day")):
    truth_panel(ax, 16, predictor, oracle=False)
    ax.set_xlabel("years from campaign")
    ax.set_ylabel(ylab)
axes[0].plot([], [], color=TRUTH, lw=3.4, label="malariasimulation")
axes[0].plot([], [], color=PIPELINE, lw=1.8, label="MINTverse")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![A held-out, strongly seasonal parameter set under a net campaign. The white line is malariasimulation, averaged over the individual stochastic runs drawn in grey. The red line is MINTverse, starting from a measured prevalence.](overview_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-1.png){fig-alt='Two panels, prevalence and clinical cases over seven years, both oscillating sharply with the season. The red MINTverse prediction lies on top of the white simulator average throughout, before and after the campaign at year zero.'}
:::
:::


Across 1,954 parameter sets held out of training entirely, the emulator tracks the simulator
to a mean absolute error of 0.0044 in prevalence, which is under half a percentage point, at an
R² of 0.999 and with no systematic bias. Please see
[Accuracy and speed](../03-concepts/validation.qmd) for the trajectory-by-trajectory
comparison and for what the error costs when the EIR has to be estimated rather than known.

Note that outside its training range the emulator is not reliable, and that `estimint` clamps
out-of-range covariates silently, so a setting well beyond that range still comes back with an
answer.

## What you need to run it

The emulator is parameterised by twelve numbers. You do not supply them directly, because
`run_scenarios` derives several of them from the ones you do.

**One measure of transmission.** Exactly one of the following, whichever you have:

| You have | Pass it as | Typical source |
|---|---|---|
| Under-5 prevalence before the campaign | `EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence")` | A cross-sectional survey (DHS, MIS) |
| A human biting rate | `EirTarget(250000, "hbr")` | Entomological trapping |
| An EIR already | `EirTarget(20, "eir")` | A previous calibration |

`estimint` produces single values, not trajectories. It converts whichever of the three
measures you supply into the EIR the emulator runs from, and the EIR and HBR it reports are
equilibrium quantities at the moment the campaign starts. Only prevalence and cases have
trajectories, and those come from `stateMINT`. Please see
[EIR, HBR, prevalence, and cases](../03-concepts/equilibrium.qmd) for how the four quantities
move through the pipeline.

**The setting.** Four numbers describing the district and its mosquitoes:

| Input | What it is | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| `Q0` | Human blood index | A property of the local vector species |
| `phi` | Proportion of bites taken while people are in bed | Vector species and human behaviour |
| `seasonal` | 0 for perennial transmission, 1 for strongly seasonal | Known for the setting |
| `res_use` | Pyrethroid resistance, 0 to 1 | Bioassay data on the local vector population |

**The interventions in place now.** The current net mix, as usage shares by net type (`py_only`, `py_pbo`, `py_pyrrole`, `py_ppf`), and the current IRS coverage (`irs`).
Leave the net keys out entirely if there are no nets. You do **not** compute the net killing
effect yourself, because `calculate_dn0` turns the mix and the resistance level into the `dn0`
covariate the models consume.

**The campaign you want to evaluate.** The net type and coverage from the campaign onwards (`net_type_future`, `itn_future`), and any spraying, larviciding or routine distribution that comes with it (`irs_future`, `lsm`, `routine`).
These default to zero, which means the intervention is **withdrawn** at the campaign.

Everything else is optional. `mosquito_delta`, which describes a change in mosquito density,
has no effect on the result at its default of zero.

You do not need a GPU, a `malariasimulation` installation, R, any training data, or any
weights on disk. Installation pulls the estiMINT models with the wheel. The emulator weights
download once from Hugging Face on first use.

::: {.callout-important}
## Future coverage must be set explicitly

`itn_future`, `net_type_future` and `irs_future` describe what happens **from** the campaign,
not what is already there. Left unset, they tell the model to treat the existing nets and
spraying as **withdrawn** at the campaign. To hold an intervention steady you must restate it
in the future keys. Please see [Covariates and the time grid](../05-statemint/covariates.qmd).
:::

## Where to start

MINTverse is written for researchers studying transmission and interventions, and we assume
more familiarity with malaria epidemiology and with R than with Python or machine learning, so
where a Python idiom differs from its R counterpart in a way that matters we spell the
difference out. If Python is new, [Python for Malaria Modellers](../01-python/index.qmd)
covers the interpreter, the environment, and the notebook from scratch. Otherwise install the
packages and run a first estimate in [Getting Started](../02-getting-started/index.qmd). For
the ideas behind the models, read [Core Concepts](../03-concepts/index.qmd).
